question: Does matching both a verified causal memory passage and the annotated source turn that it represents identify a useful span for a skill? Prior paired passages sometimes generalized worse than reassigned credit labels. A target can match the donor topic without matching the evidence that made the skill useful.
training: Use the same 60 repaired training contrasts, seven surviving question contrasts and two predeclared rank stages as witness_passages. For each eligible winning-exclusive focal rank, get the donor question's annotated source turns in its own pivot session. Choose the annotated turn with the highest cosine to the normalized winning passage (first chronologically breaks ties). All unannotated turns in that donor session are competitors. Skip this rank explicitly if the pivot has no annotated turn, no competitor, or insufficient distinct competitors for a size-matched placebo. No target question, reference, future turn, reader input or generated current write is available when computing an action.
score: At one visible target utterance t let M=relu(cos(t,win))*relu(cos(t,win)-cos(t,lose)). Missing losing texts have zero vectors. Let G=relu(cos(t,chosen_source)-max_cosine_to_unannotated_donor_turns). Use M*G, maximized jointly over target utterances and ranks for each donor question. Apply the same necessary/sufficient rank weights as the passage parent. Compare to G alone, M alone on the same eligible subset, to the parent on all eligible ranks, to rotated signed question labels and to a placebo replacing each annotated turn by the nearest following unused non-annotated turn, wrapping in chronological order. For the placebo the remaining turns (including original annotations) form the competitors. Calibrate each metric for each donor against 32 sessions (5–12) from four training histories excluding both donor and held history. Count ties in the upper tail and combine the strongest positive and negative signed case effects, exactly as the parent model. Freeze all 128 source-only session offsets before additional evaluation.
returns: At actual reached predecision states apply these offsets to the frozen repaired raw-return anchor. Use the physical 12 early four-path windows/91 questions, later 12 donor windows/88 questions as they reach all four paths, and 40 chronological randomized windows/378 questions; also track the independent-backend 40-window four-path replication. Report later assigned-pivot F1 and joint Horvitz-Thompson returns separately from exact all-path returns. A prospective window at each stage requires that neither the original nor replica had even one scored path at its numeric freeze. Do not mix scores across backends.
localization: For every complete physical window decompose the per-question exact gain versus raw and native. First multiply the first-action probability shift by the root F1 advantage with the anchor's conditional continuation. Then weight the two conditional last-action shifts times their observed F1 advantages by the new first-action occupancy. Verify the sum equals the difference of the four-path expected returns question by question. Report helpful and harmful shifts, average magnitude, and F1 by stage, dialogue and question category. On the randomized panel only the local fixed-background advantage is observed. Report the same allocation measurements for the existing parent on these same windows.
decision: The group stage is diagnostic. Full single-rank actor requires all 32 interventions. To advance require all 40 chronologically later windows, >=.02 focal F1 above native and terminal, positive joint HT above both, positive focal gain above raw, placebo, evidence-only, eligible-passage-only, parent, rotated and matched-rate, a win versus matched rate in >=4 histories, and positive strict prospective gain above native and raw. Require positive exact gain above raw and native on the completed later four-path replication. Then run independent development before the locked full LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S tests.
reference: Kakade and Langford (ICML 2002), Approximately Optimal Approximate Reinforcement Learning. The two-step decomposition is an application of the performance difference identity. https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~pabbeel/cs287-fa09/readings/KakadeLangford-icml2002.pdf
